pattern_stance_changes.reason: Both spec-first conditions beat the no-spec condition under the same teacher, scaffold and budget: the full PRD beat the direct rewrite (0.690) and the PRD-derived query beat a direct rewrite of similar median length (0.866, 235 vs 227.5 tokens) (Table 2, App D). The downside the review cites, that handing over the whole spec loses to a short brief, concerns how much structured requirement text to deliver, which is P34 and is correctly tagged mixed there. One teacher, one rollout and seed-referenced human judgments limit the strength, not the direction.

The LLM agent verifier is the scoring instrument, and its only validation is rank agreement across three verifier families (Spearman 0.964/0.976, Table 5) plus a qualitative statement that humans 'broadly track' it. There is no isolating comparison in which the judge helps or hurts an outcome, so under stance discipline this is 'introduces'.

Fine-tuned vs untuned with everything else fixed is an isolating comparison for the fine-tuning pattern, and it is positive on both dense backbones, all three benchmarks and all three verifiers (Table 5: +17.85/+18.06/+18.91 and +2.76/+1.78/+2.66), with blinded human preference in the same direction and E2/E6 MoE checkpoints preferred to the official post-trained model (0.664/0.807, Table 3). The missing data-matched control limits what can be credited to GameGo's spec pipeline, not whether fine-tuning helped.

missed_issues: The direct-query baseline is not a like-for-like control for the spec pipeline: direct queries are one-shot seed rewrites by DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp with no validator or revision loop (App D), while task-specific queries pass independent LLM fidelity and freedom validators with iterative refinement (§3.3, App C.4), so the 0.866 preference mixes spec-first planning with extra rewrite effort and a different rewrite model.

The paper attributes the full-PRD loss to degraded instruction following and lost design freedom (§1, §3.3) but reports no per-condition render rate, failure analysis or budget-exhaustion count; a 9,136-token PRD that includes a full asset contract may simply exhaust the shared execution budget, which would be a different lesson.

Outside its own benchmark the weaker-backbone gain is mostly visual: on Cookie-Bench-G Qwen3.5-27B moves from 64.25 to 65.50 on functionality but from 56.63 to 69.88 on aesthetics, and on GameGoBench part of the gain is execution rate (91.80 -> 98.29) (Table 1).

Table 3's MoE preferences count only pairs in which both games are playable (N 108-123 of 124), so a checkpoint's failures to produce a playable game are not penalised, and Fig. 8 reports early-epoch drops in primary success that this conditioning hides.

The 'dynamic constraint satisfaction' grounding (§3.2) uses no constraint solver; 'activity' and 'compatibility' constraints are labels for prompted stages with schema checks and one bounded revision (App H.1, H.5).
note: I agree with the verdict, the claim strengths and the review's main criticisms (undisclosed teacher, one rollout, in-distribution GameGoBench, overstated frontier parity and release). My blind scores were one point higher on rigor, reproducibility and generalizability, and I rated COI low rather than medium; the merge keeps the review's stricter values and I accept them. I move P14 to supports because both spec-first conditions beat the no-spec rewrite, and the 'too much spec' effect belongs to P34, which stays mixed. P18 drops to introduces because only verifier-to-verifier rank agreement is shown, and P25 rises to supports because fine-tuning beat the untuned base on every backbone, benchmark and verifier. Beyond the review, the direct-query control was written by a different model without the validator loop, the full-PRD loss has no failure analysis, and the out-of-distribution gain for the weaker backbone is mainly aesthetics.
